lines: Welcome to Module Five: Evaluation.
It's about measuring what your model can actually do.
Picture a team that fine-tunes a small model for customer support.
Validation loss falls, the demo looks great, and they ship on Friday.
By Monday, the tickets are piling up.
The answers sound confident, but they quote the wrong refund policy.
Worse, a benchmark score jumped, and nobody can explain why.
Some test questions had leaked into the training data.
The fix isn't one magic number.
It's a set of measurements, each matched to a question.
Lesson one starts with the metrics.
Loss curves show whether training worked, and perplexity turns loss into an intuitive number.
BLEU and ROUGE count words that overlap with a reference answer.
But overlap can't see a wrong number, so a fluent, false answer still scores well.

say.0: Blue and rouge count words that overlap with a reference answer.

lines: When answers are checkable, use exact match, or pass@k, which runs generated code against tests.
Multiple-choice benchmarks score each option by its log-likelihood.

lines: You'll see which knobs silently change the numbers, like shot count and chat template.
Between runs, change exactly one thing: the model.
And you'll catch contamination by checking n-gram overlap with benchmark questions.
At scale, NeMo Evaluator runs these checks against any served model.

lines: Lesson three tackles open-ended answers with no single reference.
An LLM judge scores them with a rubric, and swapping answer order cancels position bias.

say.1: An L L M judge scores them with a rubric, and swapping answer order cancels position bias.

lines: A judge is a model too, so you check it against human labels.
Cohen's kappa measures agreement beyond pure chance.
For RAG systems, you evaluate retrieval and generation separately.
Faithfulness asks whether every claim is backed by the retrieved context.
